newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy approves return of Nazi looted gold to Jews.
newsitem.headline: Italy approves return of Nazi looted gold to Jews.

text.p: Italy said on Wednesday it would return gold and valuables, which turned up in a Treasury vault earlier this year, to the Jewish communities from which they were looted by occupying Nazi forces during World War Two.

The Treasury Ministry said in a statement that the Senate (upper house) had given final approval to a government bill sponsored by Treasury Ministry Carlo Azeglio Ciampi to hand over the treasures to the Union of Italian Jewish Communities.
The Treasury set up a commission in February to assess who owned the gold and other objects that had apparently been stripped from Jews at a Nazi death camp in northern Italy.

"The extremely speedy approval of the law, around a month and a half, is of great moral significance and puts our country among the first to take legal steps to fulfil a duty of civility and solidarity towards the Jewish communities," it said.

The valuables, contained in five crates deposited with the Treasury for safekeeping 35 years ago, included gold watches, coins, jewels, family silver, necklaces, rings, bracelets, trays, cutlery, precious stones and some false teeth in gold.
The Treasury said that documents obtained by the investigating commission showed the objects were taken by Nazi troops from Jews near the Adriatic coast of northeastern Italy.

The city of Trieste was under Nazi occupation from September 1943 until the end of the war in 1945 and many of the city's Jews perished at the nearby Risiera di San Sabba, the only German Nazi death camp in Italy.

The Treasury said the plundered treasure was moved to Klagenfurt in Austria by the retreating Germans at the end of World War Two and was later returned to Trieste, where some of the valuables were returned to their owners.
Those whose owners could not be traced were deposited with a bank in Trieste, and then in the province's own official vaults, before being sent to the Treasury in Rome in 1962.

The valuables were traced to the Treasury by the prefect, or central government representative, of Trieste, Michele De Feis, who launched an inquiry last year into the whereabouts of the missing treasure after Trieste's Jewish community raised a claim for compensation for victims of the Holocaust.
Their case followed public controversy over whether Swiss banks kept millions of dollars deposited in secret accounts by Jews before and during the war.
The statement said the valuables would be handed over for return to the Jewish communities from where they were looted as soon as the bill was published in the official gazette.
